title: ALPFA NJIT App
summary: A chapter mobile app for finding events, meeting the E-Board, and sharing photos.
role: E-Board content updates and app support
scope: Collaborative chapter app · Timeline not documented
verifiedContribution: Added member information and headshots, updated profiles, and contributed error fixes.
overview: A collaborative mobile app for the ALPFA NJIT chapter, bringing chapter events, E-Board profiles, and photo sharing into one place.

sections.title: The problem
sections.text: Give chapter members a convenient place to find events, learn about the E-Board, and engage with the chapter.

sections.title: My contribution
sections.text: I contributed E-Board member information and headshots, including image updates and profile changes. I also worked on error fixes. The GitHub repository belongs to my project partner, AnabhayanA.

sections.title: What the team built
sections.text: The app code includes chapter calendar events and reminders, an E-Board directory, and a capture flow for selecting or taking photos and sharing them through a backend. The camera flow includes filters and optional location labels.

sections.title: Status & limitations
sections.text: The project documentation says core features are implemented, with final visual polish, cross-device QA, and production builds still ahead. The separately deployed backend is not included in the repository; I did not retest its integrations for this portfolio.

cardContribution: I added E-Board member information and headshots and worked on error fixes.

title: ZipHeatMap
summary: A ZIP-code mapping tool I developed to show where the department’s donors are concentrated.
scope: Individual departmental tool · Timeline not documented
verifiedContribution: Built the MATLAB ZIP-code validation, filtering, and heat-map workflow used to communicate donor distribution.
overview: I developed ZipHeatMap for my University Advancement operations work. It turns donor ZIP-code data into geographic heat maps so staff can see where most donors are concentrated and present the distribution to leadership at a high level.

sections.title: The problem
sections.text: ZIP-code records alone made it difficult to see where donors were concentrated across the United States. My department needed a clear geographic view it could use in presentations to leadership.

sections.title: My contribution
sections.text: I developed the MATLAB application to check ZIP-code data, match it to reference coordinates, filter and summarize results, and generate heat maps that communicate donor concentration at a glance.

sections.title: How it works
sections.text: The application matches ZIP codes against a reference spreadsheet, flags invalid or unmatched entries, and summarizes data by state. Staff can filter locations, view ZIP-code frequency on a heat map, and export a map image or plotted data for presentations.

sections.title: Checks & limitations
sections.text: I used the maps to show donor distribution in presentations for department leadership. I have not documented usage counts, measured time savings, or a decision made from the maps. The packaged Windows app was not rerun for this portfolio and requires MATLAB Runtime R2025b.

sections.title: Privacy
sections.text: The portfolio describes the workflow without publishing donor records, input spreadsheets, or maps based on donor data.

cardContribution: I built maps of donor concentration by ZIP code for department presentations.

title: Tempo
summary: A collaborative planner that turns tasks, available time, and commitments into a reviewable schedule.
role: Database setup, API checks, and rebuild review
scope: Collaborative hackathon origin · Local rebuild ongoing
verifiedContribution: Configured PostgreSQL connectivity, checked FastAPI operations, and reviewed planning work in the rebuild.
overview: Tempo started as a collaborative planning project. Its newer local rebuild combines task and calendar planning with an optional Gemini assistant.

sections.title: The problem
sections.text: Help people fit tasks around commitments and deadlines while keeping them in control of the resulting plan.

sections.title: My contribution
sections.text: For the earlier hackathon version, I configured PostgreSQL connectivity and checked FastAPI operations. I also worked with a coding agent on the newer rebuild, reviewing the planning and calendar work and its documented checks.

sections.title: Design decisions
sections.text: The rebuild uses a deterministic planner that works without an AI key. People review proposed changes before applying them; calendar files and subscribed feeds are snapshots, not instant two-way sync.

sections.title: What was checked
sections.text: The rebuild’s notes report unit, database, and desktop/mobile browser checks, including tests using simulated services. Live checks documented successful calendar flows as well as a later Gemini provider outage; they do not establish a clean full live desktop pass. For this portfolio, a mocked manual-planning flow was run locally to capture the interface with fictional data.

sections.title: Version & limitations
sections.text: The local Next.js rebuild is ahead of its published branch and has not been deployed to production. The default repository link opens the earlier React/Vite and FastAPI version; the linked rebuild branch may not include the latest local changes.

cardContribution: I configured database connectivity, checked FastAPI operations, and worked with a coding agent on the rebuild.

title: Echo Mountain
summary: A top-down snowboarding game with changing courses, obstacles, and local run records.
scope: Local browser-game prototype · Timeline not documented
verifiedContribution: Project records document a playable prototype and 19 automated tests; individual authorship is not established.
overview: A browser-based snowboarding prototype where players choose a trail, steer around obstacles, and build a score on the way down.
cardContribution: Choose a difficulty, time of day, and optional expert fog.

sections.title: The idea
sections.text: Create a downhill game that makes each run feel different through difficulty, time-of-day settings, and changing obstacles.

sections.title: What it includes
sections.text: Players steer with a keyboard or touch controls, choose a difficulty and time of day, use ramps, and try to avoid obstacles. Expert mode includes optional fog.

sections.title: Scoring & records
sections.text: Time, close calls, and ramps contribute to the score and multiplier. Previous and longest-run markers are stored in the current browser.

sections.title: What was checked
sections.text: The local prototype was run in a browser for these screenshots. Its 19 automated tests passed, covering rules, generated courses, jumps, fog, and records.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.text: This is a local prototype; the available copy does not establish a public deployment or document individual contribution history. Browser-local records can be lost when browser data is cleared.

title: Rock, Paper, Scissors
summary: A small game with a bigger question: how do you know a result is right?
scope: Individual IS218 coursework · Timeline not documented
verifiedContribution: Defined checks, requested history and streak features, and reviewed gameplay and keyboard replay.
overview: A browser-based game for playing a round against the computer, with recent history and session streaks.

sections.title: The problem
sections.text: Make each round understandable and dependable: show both moves, return the right outcome, and let someone play again.

sections.title: My contribution & process
sections.text: I agreed on the rules and checks, requested the recent-history and streak extensions, and reviewed a round and keyboard replay. A coding agent implemented changes from the provided starter and ran checks; the project record separates that assistance from my own observations.

sections.title: Decisions
sections.text: Rounds stay independent. Recent games and streaks are kept in a temporary browser session rather than a database or account.

sections.title: What was checked
sections.text: The project record reports checks for all nine outcomes, invalid input, request behavior, and browser replay. Its final local run recorded 38 non-browser and 10 Chromium tests passing, alongside formatting and lint checks.

sections.title: Limitation & next step
sections.text: Refreshing a completed submission can replay the last move. A redirect after submission is a documented follow-up. The record distinguishes automated checks from the round I personally reviewed.

cardContribution: I agreed on the rules and checks, requested extensions, and reviewed gameplay with coding-agent assistance.
